newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius needs sugar reforms for competitive edge.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius needs sugar reforms for competitive edge.

text.p: Mauritian agriculture authorities said the centralisation of sugar mills was unavoidable if the Indian Ocean island was to keep a competitive edge in the global market.
Agriculture Minister Arvind Boolell also called for the full use of existing spare capacity to reduce fixed costs.
Boolell's comments were contained in a government blueprint for sugar mill reforms. The blueprint, from the agriculture ministry, was passed to Reuters at the weekend.

"It is imperative that in the 1995 to 2001 grace period of stable nominal prices the sugar industry reduces its cost of production, optimises the use of by-products and improves health and safety at the workplace," Boolell said.
The centralisation process would enable the installation of modern, more efficient and larger-sized equipment geared towards energy-saving and energy generation from bagasse.
Boolell would not say whether any sugar mills would be shut, only that if mill owners thought their business was no longer viable then they would formally request closure.
But the blueprint made provision for compensation of workers who might become redundant through closure.
Redundant workers would be offered the choice of either employment in other sugar factories or a package comprising a cash compensation, a portion of land, a training grant and a business plan grant.
"The modernisation and restructuring programme will also cater for human aspects. The debate is how to harmonise social and political issues with economic imperatives," Boolell said.
He added that the government of Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam would be acting as facilitator in the implementation of the centralisation programme.
The Mauritius Sugar Authority, which falls under the agriculture ministry, would be responsible for the overall implementation.
Sugar industry officials say consolidation of sugar mills from the present 17 to 14 or less by the year 2000 is essential to improve competitiveness.
Under the Sugar Protocol of the Lome Convention, Mauritius has an annual 510,000 tonnes export quota to the European Union at guaranteed prices that are higher than world market prices.
After the expiry of the Lome Convention in the year 2000 sugar prices will no longer be guaranteed.
